title: Security: WPA3 and Wi-Fi 7
summary: Stronger sign-in that resists password guessing, required on 6 GHz and for Wi-Fi 7 multi-link.
wifi7Adds: WPA3 arrived alongside Wi-Fi 6 {{wpa3-mandatory-cert}}; Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connections require it {{wpa3-mlo-required}}, and the 6 GHz band does not permit WPA2 {{wpa3-6ghz-required}}.

beats.heading: One captured handshake, unlimited guesses
beats.body:
Many clinical device networks still use a shared passphrase with [[wpa2|WPA2]]-Personal. Someone in the car park can record the moment a device joins, take that recording away, and try millions of passphrase guesses offline — no one on the network would ever notice {{wpa3-sae}}.

If they succeed, they can join the network and, with the passphrase, potentially decrypt traffic they recorded earlier.
beats.bottomLine: A single weak or long-lived shared passphrase can expose a whole device network, often without any sign of an attack.
beats.sceneDescription: A device joins an access point while an outside observer records the exchange. The observer carries the recording away to a separate machine, where a lock icon rapidly cycles through guesses until it springs open.

beats.heading: WPA3: a handshake that gives nothing away
beats.body:
[[wpa3|WPA3]] replaces the WPA2-Personal handshake with [[sae|SAE]], an exchange designed so that a recording is useless for offline guessing: every guess requires talking to the real network {{wpa3-sae}}. WPA3 is required for new Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices {{wpa3-mandatory-cert}}.

For open networks such as guest Wi-Fi, [[owe|Wi-Fi Enhanced Open]] encrypts traffic without a password {{owe-what}}.
beats.bottomLine: WPA3 closes the most common way attackers break shared-passphrase networks, and it is already built into current devices.
beats.sceneDescription: The device and the access point exchange messages that the observer can still record, but the recording now produces a sealed box that cannot be tested offline, and the observer's guesses go nowhere.

beats.heading: Fresh keys every session
beats.body:
With SAE, both sides prove they know the password without revealing anything an eavesdropper can test, and they agree on a fresh encryption key for each session {{wpa3-sae}}.

That gives [[forward-secrecy|forward secrecy]]: even if the password leaks later, traffic captured earlier stays protected {{wpa3-forward-secrecy}}. WPA3 also protects management frames, which stops simple attacks that knock devices off the network.
beats.bottomLine: A leaked password no longer means every past recording can be decrypted, which limits the damage of a single mistake.
beats.deepDive: SAE is a password-authenticated key exchange (the "dragonfly" handshake) followed by the standard 4-way handshake; each successful exchange yields a unique pairwise key {{wpa3-sae}}. WPA3 configurations require protected management frames (PMF), and WEP, TKIP and WPA version 1 are disallowed {{legacy-security-disallowed}}. Hash-to-element (H2E) derives the password element in constant time, closing side channels found in early SAE implementations {{wifi7-eht-security}}.
beats.sceneDescription: Each device that joins receives its own differently coloured lock, showing a unique key per session. An old recording on the observer's machine stays locked even after a password card appears.

beats.heading: Required where it matters most
beats.body:
With earlier Wi-Fi, WPA3 was optional and many networks stayed on WPA2. The 6 GHz band does not permit WPA2-Personal at all {{wpa3-6ghz-required}}, and Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connections require WPA3 {{wpa3-mlo-required}}.

For Wi-Fi 7 networks, Wi-Fi Alliance deployment guidance goes further, making beacon protection and the strongest encryption options mandatory {{wifi7-eht-security}}.
beats.bottomLine: Moving to Wi-Fi 7 and 6 GHz is also a security upgrade: the strongest settings become the baseline rather than an option someone has to remember.
beats.deepDive: For networks with EHT enabled, the WPA3 deployment guide marks as mandatory: the SAE-GDH AKM (suite 24), PMF required, SAE hash-to-element only, beacon protection, and both GCMP-256 and CCMP-128 pairwise ciphers {{wifi7-eht-security}}. A [[mld|multi-link device]] negotiates one security association that applies to all of its links {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. [[beacon-protection|Beacon protection]] lets devices detect forged beacons. These are deployment requirements, not certification rules, so confirm configuration options with each product.
beats.sceneDescription: Two gates stand side by side. The earlier generation's gate admits devices using WPA2 or WPA3. The Wi-Fi 7 and 6 GHz gate admits only WPA3 devices and turns a WPA2 device away.

beats.heading: Protecting clinical and device traffic
beats.body:
Hospital networks carry clinical messages, device [[telemetry|telemetry]] and staff communications. Stronger sign-in and per-session encryption make it much harder to eavesdrop on or impersonate that traffic.

WPA3 is one layer of security, not a complete programme: it complements network segmentation, device management and your organisation's security and compliance processes.
beats.bottomLine: Plan WPA3 alongside clinical device refresh: some older devices may not support it, so 6 GHz and Wi-Fi 7 networks may need separate network names during the transition.
beats.sceneDescription: Clinical devices — a voice badge, an infusion pump and a monitor — each hold their own lock while connected to the access point, and the outside observer gives up and fades away.

keyFigures.note: Earlier generations have no multi-link operation.
